translations.text: ...remembrance. But my slayer is prayer, with hope of those eternal good things.
And as for who gave birth to prayer, ask it yourselves, for it sings to the Lord and calls upon him. To him be glory to the ages of ages.
Amen. This is the thirteenth [step]. It is victory over the passions. Whoever wins this victory has been proven in all things.
Composed by the same holy father of ours, John of Sinai. On gluttony. Chapter 14. I wish to speak a little about gluttony too,
as about those other passions. But we direct these words against ourselves, we who speak about the greed of the belly, for I would be amazed
if anyone had become free of it before taking up residence in the grave. Gluttony is the hypocrisy of the belly: when it is full, it claims to be in want,
and when it is filled and bursting, it cries out that it is hungry, and eagerly seeks to take in still more food. Gluttony is the inventor of foods

and the source of the love of tasty things. When you have stopped up one of its springs, it breaks out somewhere else, and when you have dried that one up too, it overpowers you somewhere else. Gluttony deceives the eyes,
for the belly holds little, yet gluttony suggests that one could swallow everything at once. Being full of food is the father of fornication,
but the affliction [?] of the belly is the guide to purity. Whoever gives rest to a lion often tames it,
but whoever gives rest to the flesh makes it even fiercer. The Jew rejoices over the Sabbath and the feast, and the gluttonous monk over Saturday and Sunday.
He counts up the feasting a year [?] in advance, and prepares the foods before the time comes. The slave of the belly thinks about what foods he will celebrate the feast with,
but the true servant of God thinks about what divine graces he will be enriched with. When a stranger comes to the glutton, he welcomes him with joy,
sets the table at once, and counts his own breaking of the fast as love for his brother. When some visitors come, he decides to allow wine,
and thinks that he is hiding his virtue, but he is a slave of passion. Vainglory is often hostile to gluttony,
and they quarrel over the wretched monk like two masters over a purchased slave. The one forces him to relax the rule,
and the other compels him to show off his virtue. The wise monk escapes them both, for at the right time he drives out one with the other. When the battles of the flesh overpower us,
then let us torment the flesh at every time and in every place. But if we have put the flesh to death (and I do not know that this has ever happened to anyone before going to the grave),
then let us hide our virtue. I saw old priests whom the demons mocked. At banquets they would pressure young men
who were not under their obedience, and with oaths and the sign of the cross they released them to take wine and other foods
that they had given up. If such priests are well known for complete fear of God and for ascetic labor,
then because of their sign of the cross let us relax our rule a little, if we find ourselves in such a situation.
But if they are negligent, let us count their sign of the cross as nothing, especially if that fire of the flesh is overpowering us. The wretched and pitiable Evagrius thought
which was given to me: this wretched, coarse and resisting flesh. When any of these things spoken of earlier happens to us,
then let us pray to the Lord with fervour and humility. If after that prayer we still find it the same for a long time, let us know that the matter comes not from the workers,
but from nature, or else it is some providence of God, and He wants our benefit through things that oppose us,
so that He might humble our pride on every side. Severe and difficult is the searching out of that abyss of God's judgements,
for those who search out such things sail in the ship of pride. A brother asked an elder,
one of those who see hidden things, and said to him: "Why did God, though He knew beforehand that some would fall, adorn
them with gifts and miracles?" He answered: "First, so that other souls might be made cautious; second, so that He might show the free will of human beings;
and third, so that at the judgement to come He might leave those who have fallen without excuse." The old Law, as being weak, said: "[?]";
but the Lord, as being strong, commanded us to correct our brother too, and said: "[?]" and what follows. If your joy is holy and your learning humble,
act according to the word of the Lord, and especially with those who take it upon themselves.
But if you are not of that measure, then act according to that same word of the Law, and take heed to yourself. Do not be surprised if even those you love become hostile to you,
for some are vessels of the devil, and especially against his enemies. I am amazed, beloved,
at one of our ways of acting: how for the virtues we have help from God, who is able to do all things, and from His angels and His saints;
but for evil things only the demons are our helpers, and yet we are more eager for evil things and passions. For this reason I cannot say much,
nor do I wish to. If all created things remain in the same nature in which they were created, as I am the image of God
and am mixed with this clay, as the great Gregory the Theologian says, but if any created thing is outside the nature
in which it was created, then without doubt it longs insatiably for its own proper state.
Let a person use every means and strive with all eagerness to raise up this clay and seat it on the throne of God. And let no one make excuses about that ascent,
for the way and the door have been opened. Hearing of the spiritual virtues of the fathers rouses a person's mind and soul to imitate their zeal;
and hearing their teaching in turn stirs a person to longing for them and leads them to become like them,
those who have divine zeal. Reading is a lamp in darkness, a guide to those who have gone astray, and one who gives light to the blind. The reader is one who finds health,
and one who breaks down pains and makes them vanish. Those who marvel at the small deeds of others do so for one of two reasons:
either from great lack of understanding, or from great humility they magnify and exalt their neighbour's deeds. Let us strive not only to fight
but also to defeat the demons, for whoever fights sometimes wins and sometimes is defeated;
